author: Author uncertain; traditionally Moses; many scholars see later sources and editing
authorNote: Genesis names no writer. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses with all five books of the Law: the Talmud says so (Bava Batra 14b), and the New Testament speaks of ‘the book of Moses’ and ‘the law of Moses’ (Mark 12:26; Luke 24:44, KJV). Many modern scholars, classically following Julius Wellhausen, see the five books as earlier sources (often labelled J, E, D and P) edited into a final form around the 6th–5th c. BC; that model is now much debated, and conservative scholars hold Moses to be the original author, with some later updating.
date: Events c. 2000–1600 BC (patriarchs); composition traditionally 15th c. BC; many scholars date its final form to the 6th–5th c. BC
audience: Israel on the edge of the promised land, needing to know who their God is and where they came from
setting: Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt in the Middle Bronze Age; a world of city-states, clan migration and covenant treaties
purpose: To ground Israel's identity in the God who created the world, chose Abraham, and kept his promises through failure and famine
themes: Promise of land, seed and blessing
outline: Primeval history: creation, fall, flood, Babel
Joseph and the move to Egypt

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Moses; many scholars see later sources and editing
authorNote: Exodus does not name the writer of the whole book, though it records Moses being told to write, and writing, particular words and laws (17:14; 24:4; 34:27). The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) and the New Testament (Mark 12:26; Luke 24:44) credit the books of the Law to Moses. Many modern scholars see several sources edited into a final form around the 6th–5th c. BC, a model now much debated; conservative scholars hold Moses to be the original author, with some later updating.
date: Exodus c. 1491 BC (Ussher, as dated here); others c. 1446 BC (early) or c. 1270 BC (late)
audience: The generation of Israel formed into a nation at Sinai
setting: New Kingdom Egypt (a pharaoh of the 18th or 19th dynasty), the Sinai wilderness
purpose: To show how YHWH redeemed Israel from slavery, bound them to himself by covenant, and came to dwell among them
outline: Tabernacle instructions, golden calf, tabernacle built

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Moses; many scholars see later sources and editing
authorNote: Leviticus names no writer; it presents its laws as given by the LORD to Moses at Sinai (1:1; 27:34). The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) and the New Testament (Mark 12:26; Luke 24:44) credit the books of the Law to Moses. Scholars who trace sources assign it to the Priestly (P) material, gathered from various periods and put together perhaps during or after the exile, with its Holiness Code (chapters 17–26) often dated to the exile, by some earlier; conservative scholars hold Moses to be the original author.
date: Received at Sinai, c. 1490 BC (Ussher); others c. 1446 or 1270 BC
audience: Priests and people of Israel camped at Sinai
setting: The newly built tabernacle; a holy God now dwells in the middle of the camp
purpose: To teach how sinful people can live in the presence of a holy God through sacrifice, priesthood and holiness

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Moses; many scholars see later sources and editing
authorNote: Numbers names no writer, though it says Moses wrote down the stages of Israel’s journeys (33:2). The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) credits Moses with the Torah, naming Balaam’s story (22–24) in particular. Many modern scholars see a composite of the J, E and Priestly (P) sources, edited into the five books by about the 5th c. BC; conservative scholars hold Moses to be the original author, with some later updating.
date: Events c. 1490–1451 BC (Ussher); others c. 1446–1406 or 1270–1230 BC
audience: The second wilderness generation about to enter Canaan
setting: Forty years of wandering from Sinai to the plains of Moab
purpose: To record the failure of the first generation and God's faithfulness in preparing the second
outline: New generation prepares for the land

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Moses; many scholars tie its core to Josiah’s reform, c. 622 BC
authorNote: Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses’ speeches in Moab and says he wrote ‘this law’ (1:1–5; 31:9, KJV), but a narrator frames them and chapter 34 tells of his death; the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) records a dispute over its last eight verses (34:5–12), written by Joshua on one view and by Moses in tears on the other. Many modern scholars tie its core (chapters 12–26) to the law book found in the Temple under Josiah, c. 622 BC (2 Kings 22), with additions through the exile. Conservative scholars hold Moses to be the original author.
date: Plains of Moab, c. 1451 BC (Ussher; others c. 1406 or 1230 BC); many scholars date its composition from the 8th c. BC to the exile and beyond, its core tied to the law book found c. 622 BC
audience: Israel about to cross the Jordan without Moses
setting: Moab, east of the Jordan; structured like an ancient Near-Eastern suzerain–vassal treaty
purpose: To renew the covenant and call a new generation to love and obey YHWH in the land
themes: Love the LORD with all your heart (the Shema)

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Joshua; many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th c. BC
authorNote: Joshua names no writer, though it says Joshua wrote words ‘in the book of the law of God’ (24:26, KJV), and it goes on to record his death. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b–15a) says Joshua wrote the book and that Eleazar, then Phinehas, finished it. Many modern scholars, following Martin Noth, see older traditions edited into a history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, addressed to a late pre-exilic audience on some views and completed after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC on others.
date: Events c. 1451–1427 BC (as dated here); others from c. 1406 BC or in the 13th c. BC
audience: Israel settled in the land, remembering how it was given
setting: Late Bronze Age Canaan: fortified city-states in decline, Egyptian influence waning
purpose: To show God keeping his land promise and to call Israel to faithful covenant loyalty

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Samuel; many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th c. BC
authorNote: Judges names no writer. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) says Samuel wrote it, along with Ruth and his own book. Many modern scholars see older stories of the judges, oral and perhaps written, framed by a later historian within the history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, which they date from the late pre-exilic period to after 586 BC.
date: Events c. 1420–1120 BC (Ussher); others c. 1380–1050 BC
setting: Tribal Israel with no central government, pressured by Canaanites, Midianites and Philistines
purpose: To show the downward spiral of a people who do what is right in their own eyes, and God's repeated mercy
themes: Cycle of sin, oppression, cry, deliverance
Israel's need for a righteous king

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Samuel; scholars date it to the early monarchy or after the exile
authorNote: Ruth names no writer. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) says Samuel wrote it; its closing genealogy ends with David (4:17–22), which some scholars take as a later addition. Many date the book early in the monarchy, others after the exile (5th–4th c. BC), citing its language and reading its warm portrait of a Moabite woman as a counter to Ezra and Nehemiah’s measures against such marriages.
date: Set in the judges period, c. 1308 BC (as dated here); written later, early in the monarchy or after the exile (5th–4th c. BC); scholars differ
audience: Israel in the monarchy, curious about David's Moabite roots
setting: Bethlehem and Moab during a famine; agricultural life, kinsman-redeemer customs
purpose: To show God's hidden providence and covenant loyalty (hesed) working through ordinary faithfulness, and to trace David's line

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Samuel, then Gad and Nathan; many scholars see later editing
authorNote: The book names no author; 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book, and 1 Chronicles 29:29 mentions books of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b–15a) says Samuel wrote it and, because it records his death, Gad and Nathan finished it. Many modern scholars see a work built from earlier sources, such as the ark story and the story of David’s succession, and given its final form by a Deuteronomistic compiler in the 6th c. BC.
date: Events c. 1165–1056 BC (Ussher); others c. 1100–1010 BC
audience: Israel reflecting on the birth of the monarchy
setting: Transition from judges to kings under Philistine pressure
purpose: To show how Israel got a king and why God rejected Saul and chose David
themes: The LORD looks at the heart

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Gad and Nathan; many scholars see later editing
authorNote: The book names no author; it is the second half of the one book of Samuel. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says Samuel wrote that book and that, since it records his death in 1 Samuel, Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet finished it. Many modern scholars see it as built from earlier sources, notably the story of David’s court and succession, and given its final form by a Deuteronomistic compiler in the 6th c. BC.
date: Events c. 1055–1015 BC (Ussher); others c. 1010–970 BC
setting: David's reign: Jerusalem captured, kingdom united and expanded
purpose: To narrate David's reign honestly—his triumphs, God's covenant with him, and the consequences of his sin
themes: God's grace to a flawed king
outline: Sin with Bathsheba and family turmoil

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Jeremiah; many scholars: part of the Deuteronomistic History
authorNote: The book names no author but cites earlier records of Solomon’s reign and of the kings of Israel and Judah. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says Jeremiah wrote it. Since Martin Noth (1943) many scholars have read Deuteronomy to Kings as one ‘Deuteronomistic History’ finished in the exile after 561 BC, some (following Frank Moore Cross) seeing a first edition under Josiah.
date: Events c. 1015–897 BC (Ussher); others c. 970–850 BC; final form in the exile (after 561 BC)
audience: Exiles asking why the kingdom fell
setting: Solomon's empire, then the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah
purpose: To evaluate each king by covenant faithfulness and explain the road to exile

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Jeremiah; many scholars: part of the Deuteronomistic History
authorNote: The book names no author and, like 1 Kings, cites the royal records of the kings of Israel and Judah. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says Jeremiah wrote Kings. Since Martin Noth (1943) many scholars have read Deuteronomy to Kings as one ‘Deuteronomistic History’, finished in the exile after Jehoiachin’s release in 561 BC (25:27), some (following Frank Moore Cross) seeing a first edition under Josiah.
date: Events c. 896–562 BC (Ussher); others c. 850–561 BC; final form in the exile (after 561 BC)
setting: Assyrian conquest of Israel (722 BC), Babylonian conquest of Judah (586 BC)
purpose: To show that exile was covenant judgement, yet leave a flicker of hope in the Davidic line
outline: Judah's last kings and fall of Jerusalem

author: Author uncertain; ‘the Chronicler’, traditionally Ezra, then Nehemiah; many scholars doubt this
authorNote: The book names no author; its writer is known as ‘the Chronicler’, and 1 and 2 Chronicles were originally one book. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says Ezra wrote its genealogies up to his own time and Nehemiah completed it, but many scholars doubt this tradition and date the book to the 4th c. BC. Scholars long held that the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah; many now treat them as separate works.
date: Probably 4th c. BC; mid-5th c. BC if by Ezra
audience: Post-exilic community rebuilding identity around temple and Davidic hope
setting: Persian-period Judah, a small province around a rebuilt temple
purpose: To retell Israel's story emphasising David, worship and continuity with the past

author: Author uncertain; ‘the Chronicler’, traditionally Ezra, then Nehemiah; many scholars doubt this
authorNote: The book names no author; it is the second half of the one book of Chronicles, whose writer is known as ‘the Chronicler’. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) credits Ezra, with Nehemiah completing the work, but many scholars doubt this and date the book to the 4th c. BC. Its closing verses repeat the opening of Ezra, long taken as a sign of a single author, a view some still hold; many now treat Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah as separate works.
date: Probably 4th c. BC; mid-5th c. BC if by Ezra
setting: Same as 1 Chronicles; covers Solomon to the decree of Cyrus
purpose: To highlight temple worship and show that seeking God brings blessing, forsaking him brings ruin
outline: Kings of Judah to the exile and Cyrus' decree

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Ezra; many scholars see a later compiler using his memoir
authorNote: The book names no author; in Hebrew tradition Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, the book of Ezra, which the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says Ezra wrote. It includes Ezra’s memoir (chs. 7–10), told in the first person at 7:27–9:15. Many scholars credit an unnamed compiler, long identified with ‘the Chronicler’ (others now argue for a separate hand), and proposed dates run from the end of the 5th c. BC to the 3rd c. BC.
date: Events 538–457 BC; compiled with the book of Nehemiah, late 5th to 3rd c. BC
setting: Persian empire; Cyrus' decree allowing return; rebuilding the temple amid opposition
purpose: To record the return and restoration of worship and the covenant community
outline: First return under Zerubbabel; temple rebuilt

author: Author uncertain; built on Nehemiah’s memoir (named in 1:1); traditionally part of Ezra’s book
authorNote: The book opens ‘The words of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah’ (1:1, KJV), and much of it is his first-person memoir (chs. 1–7 and most of 12–13). In Hebrew tradition it was part of one book of Ezra, which the Talmud says Ezra wrote (Bava Batra 15a), though it also says Nehemiah spoke its words and asks why the book was not named after him (Sanhedrin 93b). Many scholars credit a later compiler, long identified with ‘the Chronicler’ (others now argue for a separate hand), with adding material such as Ezra’s reading of the law (ch. 8) and lists of priests and Levites (12:1–26); proposed dates run from the end of the 5th c. BC to the 3rd c. BC.
date: Events 445–430 BC; compiled with the book of Ezra, late 5th to 3rd c. BC
setting: Persian province of Yehud; Nehemiah as governor under Artaxerxes I
purpose: To show God rebuilding walls and people through prayer, leadership and covenant renewal

author: Author uncertain; traditionally the men of the Great Assembly; some medieval rabbis: Mordecai
authorNote: The book names no author. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says the men of the Great Assembly wrote it; the medieval commentators Rashi and Ibn Ezra held that Mordecai did, Rashi reading ‘And Mordecai wrote these things’ (9:20, KJV) as the book itself. Modern scholars generally treat the author as unknown and date the book anywhere from the Persian period (before 333 BC) to the 2nd c. BC.
date: Events c. 462–452 BC (Ussher); others c. 483–473 BC; written c. 465–333 BC, or as late as the 2nd c. BC
setting: Persian court at Susa under Xerxes I (Ahasuerus)
purpose: To show God's hidden providence preserving his people and to explain Purim
themes: Courage ('for such a time as this')

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Moses; the book names no writer
authorNote: The book names no writer. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) says Moses wrote it, though the rabbis there (15a–b) disagreed about when Job lived, from Jacob’s day to the return from exile, and one sage held that his story was a parable. Most modern scholars regard the author as unknown; early dates in Moses’ or Solomon’s time are not widely held today, and most place the book’s final form between the 7th and 2nd centuries BC.
date: Events often placed in the patriarchal era; by tradition written in Moses’ day, by most scholars in the 7th–2nd centuries BC
audience: Wisdom seekers wrestling with innocent suffering
setting: Land of Uz (Edom region); a non-Israelite sage
purpose: To confront simplistic retribution theology and point to trust in God's wisdom amid unexplained suffering
outline: Prologue: the LORD allows Job to be tested

author: David (73 titles), Asaph (12), sons of Korah (11), others; 50 unnamed; authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Of the 150 psalms, 116 have a title and 100 name someone: David 73 times, Asaph 12, the sons of Korah 11, Solomon twice (the KJV reads ‘for Solomon’), and Heman, Ethan and Moses once each. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b–15a) says David wrote the book, including psalms by ten elders such as Moses, Heman, Asaph and the sons of Korah, and most early church interpreters read the titles as naming the authors. Many modern scholars treat the titles as later additions and note that the Hebrew ‘of David’ can also mean ‘for’ or ‘belonging to’, so they do not take a title as proof of who wrote a psalm.
date: c. 1490–400 BC, from Moses (Psalm 90’s title) to after the exile; collected in five books
audience: Israel at worship, and every individual before God
setting: Temple worship, royal court, personal crisis, exile
purpose: To give words for every season of faith—praise, lament, thanksgiving, wisdom, kingship

author: Solomon (named in 1:1), with ‘the wise’, Agur and Lemuel; authorship widely disputed
authorNote: The book names its sources: Solomon (1:1; 10:1), ‘the words of the wise’ (22:17, KJV), proverbs of Solomon copied out by Hezekiah’s men (25:1), Agur (30:1) and King Lemuel (31:1); the closing poem on the virtuous woman (31:10–31) names no writer. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) credits Hezekiah and his colleagues with writing the book. Conservative scholars generally accept a Solomonic core compiled between about 700 and 400 BC, while critical scholars reject Solomonic authorship and commonly date chapters 1–9 after the exile; most scholars see 22:17–24:22 as drawing on the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.
date: c. 1000–700 BC for the collections it names (Solomon to Hezekiah); final form c. 700–400 BC or later
audience: Young people learning to navigate life
setting: Royal court and household instruction in Israel's wisdom tradition
purpose: To impart skill for living rooted in the fear of the LORD

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Solomon; 1:1 names only ‘the Preacher, the son of David’
authorNote: The book never names Solomon: its speaker is ‘the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem’ (1:1, KJV), and its epilogue (12:9–14) speaks of him in the third person. Tradition identifies him as Solomon (so Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1), while the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) credits Hezekiah and his colleagues with writing the book. Because of its language, with many Aramaic forms, many modern scholars, some conservatives among them, doubt that Solomon wrote it, and critical scholars date it to the 4th–3rd centuries BC.
date: c. 1000–975 BC if Solomon’s; critical scholars date it to the 4th–3rd centuries BC from its language
setting: Wisdom reflection on life 'under the sun'
purpose: To expose the vanity of life without God and call for reverent enjoyment and obedience
themes: Fear God and keep his commandments

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Solomon, from the title ‘which is Solomon’s’ (1:1)
authorNote: The title calls it the song ‘which is Solomon’s’ (1:1, KJV); the Hebrew can mean by, for or about Solomon, and the NET Bible takes it as authorship. One rabbinic tradition (Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1) has Solomon writing it in his youth, while the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) credits Hezekiah and his colleagues. Many modern scholars regard the author as unknown and date the book’s present form after the exile, though some of its poems may be as old as the 10th century BC.
date: c. 1015–975 BC if Solomon’s; many scholars date its present form after the exile, with older poems
audience: Israel celebrating covenant love and marriage
setting: Pastoral and royal imagery of ancient Israel
purpose: To celebrate love, desire and faithfulness between bride and groom; read also as Christ and his people

author: Isaiah son of Amoz (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed, especially chs. 40–66
authorNote: The book opens as ‘The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz’ (1:1, KJV), a prophet in Jerusalem from about 740 BC, and Jewish and Christian tradition received the whole book as his; John’s Gospel quotes both halves under Isaiah’s name (John 12:38–41). Critical scholars have questioned this since the late 18th century, and few now give him the whole book or even most of it: the long-standing view, going back to Bernhard Duhm, assigns chapters 40–55 to an unnamed prophet of the Babylonian exile (‘Second Isaiah’) and chapters 56–66 to later writers after the return. Conservative scholars such as J. Alec Motyer and John N. Oswalt defend the unity of the book under Isaiah.
date: c. 759–698 BC (Ussher); others c. 740–680 BC; many scholars date chs. 40–55 to the exile, 56–66 after it
audience: Judah under Assyrian threat, and future exiles
setting: Reigns of Uzziah to Hezekiah; Assyria's rise, siege of Jerusalem 701 BC
purpose: To call Judah to trust the Holy One of Israel and to announce judgement, exile and glorious restoration through the Servant

author: Jeremiah (named in 1:1), with his scribe Baruch (36:4)
authorNote: The book presents itself as ‘The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah’ (1:1, KJV), and chapter 36 tells how Baruch the scribe wrote down Jeremiah’s words as he dictated them; the Talmud likewise says Jeremiah wrote his own book (Bava Batra 15a). Scholars broadly trace the poetic oracles to Jeremiah and much of the prose narrative to Baruch, with later editors shaping the whole: the Greek text is notably shorter and arranged differently, and chapter 52, which follows ‘Thus far are the words of Jeremiah’ (51:64, KJV), closes the book with an account of Jerusalem’s fall that closely matches 2 Kings 24:18–25:30.
date: c. 627 BC to after 586 BC; ch. 52 added after c. 560 BC
audience: Judah in its final decades and the first exiles
setting: Josiah's reform, Babylon's rise, fall of Jerusalem 586 BC
purpose: To call for repentance, announce inevitable judgement, and promise a new covenant

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Jeremiah; many scholars doubt it, some see more than one poet
authorNote: The Hebrew poems name no author; the Greek Septuagint adds a preface saying that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented over Jerusalem, and the Talmud says Jeremiah wrote Lamentations (Bava Batra 15a). The attribution was universal until the 18th century; since then many scholars have doubted it on grounds of content and style, some seeing more than one poet, and most date the poems to the exile that followed the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
date: After the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC; most scholars date it before the return from exile (c. 537 BC)
setting: Ruined Jerusalem; five laments, the first four alphabetic acrostics
purpose: To grieve honestly before God while confessing his faithfulness
outline: Hope in the midst of grief

author: Ezekiel (named in 1:3)
authorNote: The book is told mostly in the first person by ‘Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi’ (1:3, KJV), an exile in Babylonia, with oracles dated from the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity (1:2) to the twenty-seventh (29:17), that is 593–571 BC. Most scholars accept the basic authenticity of the book, with additions by a school of his later followers; in the first half of the 20th century a few critics, such as C. C. Torrey, dated it much later.
setting: Jewish community by the Chebar canal in Babylon, before and after Jerusalem's fall
purpose: To show God's glory leaving the temple in judgement and returning in restoration

author: Daniel (named in 7:1); authorship and date widely disputed
authorNote: Chapters 1–6 tell of Daniel in the third person; chapter 7 says that Daniel had a dream and ‘then he wrote the dream’ (7:1, KJV), and the visions of chapters 7–12 are mostly in his own voice; Jesus speaks of ‘Daniel the prophet’ (Matthew 24:15, KJV), and the Talmud says the men of the Great Assembly wrote the book (Bava Batra 15a). The philosopher Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305) argued, as Jerome reports, that it was written in Judaea under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and most modern scholars date its final form to c. 167–164 BC, while conservative scholars such as Joyce Baldwin defend a 6th-century BC date.
date: Events 605–536 BC; traditionally written in the 6th c. BC; most scholars date the final form c. 167–164 BC
setting: Babylonian and Persian courts
purpose: To show God's sovereignty over empires and encourage faithfulness under pressure
themes: God rules the kingdoms of men
outline: Narrative: Daniel and his friends in the Babylonian and Persian courts

author: Hosea son of Beeri (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The book gives the prophecies of Hosea son of Beeri, addressed chiefly to the northern kingdom and dated by its heading to the reigns of Uzziah to Hezekiah in Judah and of Jeroboam II in Israel (1:1). The prophecies are credited to Hosea himself; some scholars see editing in Judah, including most of the heading, and some also assign chapters 4–14 to a different hand from 1–3.
date: c. 785–725 BC (Ussher); others c. 753–722 BC
setting: Israel's prosperity and decline before Assyria's conquest
purpose: To portray Israel's spiritual adultery and God's relentless covenant love

author: Joel son of Pethuel (named in 1:1)
authorNote: Little is known of Joel beyond the name of his father (1:1). Proposed dates run from the 9th century BC, under the boy-king Joash, to c. 400–350 BC; most modern scholars date the book after the exile. Many treat it as one prophet’s work, though some, following Duhm (1911), give its later part (from 2:28 in English Bibles) to a second hand.
date: Uncertain: from the 9th c. BC (under Joash) to c. 400–350 BC; most modern scholars date it after the exile
audience: Judah after a devastating locust plague
setting: Agricultural catastrophe as a foretaste of the Day of the LORD
purpose: To call for repentance and promise the outpouring of the Spirit
outline: Call to repent; promise of Spirit

author: Amos of Tekoa (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The book gives the words of Amos, a herdsman of Tekoa, from the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam II (1:1; 7:14). Modern scholarship attributes the bulk of it to Amos but sees some later additions, such as the references to Judah (2:4–5), and perhaps the closing promise of restoration (from the end of 9:8).
date: c. 787 BC (Ussher); others mid-8th c. BC, between 793 and 739 BC
audience: Prosperous northern Israel under Jeroboam II
setting: Economic boom, social injustice, religious complacency
purpose: To denounce injustice and empty worship and announce judgement

author: Obadiah (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The book presents itself as Obadiah’s vision (1:1). Nothing more is known of him, and he cannot safely be identified with any of the other men of that name in the Old Testament. Most scholars now date it after Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC and reject the 9th-century date proposed by some nineteenth-century scholars.
date: After Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC, probably before 553 BC (most reject a 9th-c. date)
setting: Edom's gloating over Jerusalem's destruction
purpose: To announce judgement on Edom and the restoration of Israel
outline: Day of the LORD and Zion

author: Author uncertain; a story about Jonah son of Amittai (1:1), told in the third person
authorNote: The book tells of the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, known from 2 Kings 14:25 in the reign of Jeroboam II, but it speaks of him in the third person and never names its writer. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) credits the men of the Great Assembly with writing down the Twelve Prophets. Proposed dates run from the 8th to the 3rd century BC: some scholars see no reason to deny that Jonah wrote it, while the best-known view links it to the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.
date: Events c. 825 BC (Ussher; under Jeroboam II, 2 Kgs 14:25), others c. 760 BC; date of writing uncertain, 8th–3rd c. BC proposed
audience: Israel resistant to God's mercy on enemies
setting: Nineveh, capital of Assyria; a great fish
purpose: To expose narrow nationalism and reveal God's compassion for all nations

author: Micah of Moresheth (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The heading names Micah the Morasthite, of Moresheth-gath (1:1, 14), and Jeremiah 26:18 recalls his preaching under Hezekiah. His ministry is not in doubt, though some critics question whether certain passages are his, and the collection may have been arranged by a later editor.
date: c. 750–700 BC (Jotham to Hezekiah)
setting: Assyrian crisis; corrupt leaders in Samaria and Jerusalem
purpose: To indict injustice and promise a ruler from Bethlehem

author: Nahum of Elkosh (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The book is headed as Nahum’s vision concerning Nineveh (1:1); nothing more is told of him. It looks back on the fall of Thebes (3:8, c. 664 BC) and forward to the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC, so it is dated between the two.
date: c. 664–612 BC (between the fall of Thebes and of Nineveh)
setting: Before Nineveh's fall in 612 BC
purpose: To announce the downfall of cruel Nineveh

author: Habakkuk (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The book names Habakkuk the prophet in its heading (1:1) and again over the prayer of chapter 3 (3:1). It is dated to Babylon’s rise, either before the end of Josiah’s reign in 609 BC or c. 605–597 BC; some scholars date it much later and regard the psalm of chapter 3 as an editor’s work.
date: c. 609–597 BC, as Babylon rose (some date it before 609)
setting: Injustice in Judah; Babylon's approaching conquest
purpose: To wrestle with why God uses the wicked and to affirm that the righteous live by faith
themes: The just shall live by faith (2:4)

author: Zephaniah son of Cushi (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The heading traces Zephaniah’s descent over four generations to a Hizkiah, perhaps King Hezekiah, and places his preaching in the reign of Josiah (1:1). Many scholars set it early in that reign, before Josiah’s reforms.
date: Under Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before his reforms; c. 630 BC (Ussher)
setting: Idolatry under Manasseh's legacy
purpose: To warn of the Day of the LORD and promise a purified remnant

author: Haggai (named in 1:1)
authorNote: The book dates Haggai’s messages to 520 BC, the second year of Darius (1:1), and reports them in the third person. An early editor framed them, and Haggai is reasonably regarded as their source; nothing is known of his family.
date: 520 BC
setting: Persian period; second year of Darius
purpose: To rouse the people to rebuild the temple

author: Zechariah son of Berechiah (named in 1:1); authorship of chapters 9–14 widely disputed
authorNote: Chapters 1–8 give Zechariah’s dated visions and sermons from 520–518 BC (1:1; 7:1). Chapters 9–14 are undated, and most critical scholars assign them to one or more later writers; others defend Zechariah’s authorship of the whole book.
date: Chapters 1–8: 520–518 BC; chapters 9–14 undated, placed by many later, in the Persian or Greek period
setting: Rebuilding of the temple; Persian rule
purpose: To encourage rebuilding and to unveil the coming Messianic king and kingdom

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Malachi (1:1), though the name may be a title, ‘my messenger’
authorNote: The heading ascribes the book to Malachi, a Hebrew word meaning ‘my messenger’ (compare 3:1). The Talmud records that the sages took it as his own name, while Rabbi Joshua ben Korha identified him with Ezra, as the Targum does. Some modern scholars read it as a title and the book as anonymous; others reply that an anonymous prophetic book would be without parallel.
date: Uncertain: c. 500–430 BC, after the temple was rebuilt; c. 430 BC (Ussher)
setting: Temple rebuilt but worship half-hearted; last prophetic voice before 400 silent years
purpose: To confront apathy and promise the coming messenger and Day of the LORD
outline: Messenger and Day of the LORD

author: Author uncertain; traditionally the apostle Matthew, the tax collector; many scholars doubt it
authorNote: The Gospel does not name its writer. Papias (quoted by Eusebius) said Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and Irenaeus said Matthew issued a Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect; the church received this Gospel as the apostle’s. Many modern scholars doubt that the apostle wrote it, chiefly because it draws heavily on Mark, while others still hold to Matthew.
setting: Roman-occupied Judea and Galilee; synagogue and church parting ways
purpose: To present Jesus as the Messiah who fulfils the Law and Prophets and founds the church

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Mark, Peter’s interpreter, identified with John Mark of Acts
authorNote: The Gospel does not name its writer; its ancient heading is ‘According to Mark’. Papias (quoted by Eusebius) and Irenaeus describe Mark as Peter’s interpreter, and tradition identifies him with John Mark of Acts, writing in Rome. Modern scholars often caution against overstating Peter’s influence, and many suggest an unknown Jewish Christian writer around AD 70.
setting: Rome under Nero, likely; fast-paced narrative for Gentile readers
purpose: To present Jesus as the suffering Son of God and Servant who gives his life as a ransom

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
authorNote: The Gospel does not name its writer; its preface, addressed to Theophilus, says the account rests on those ‘which from the beginning were eyewitnesses’ (1:2, KJV). Irenaeus and the Muratorian fragment credit it to Luke, Paul’s companion, called ‘the beloved physician’ in Colossians 4:14 (KJV). Critical scholars have been roughly evenly divided on whether that Luke wrote it, but it is widely agreed that the same writer produced Acts.
setting: Greco-Roman world; careful historical framing
purpose: To give an orderly account showing Jesus as Saviour for all people, especially the marginalised

author: Author uncertain; ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’ (21:20–24); traditionally John the apostle
authorNote: The Gospel does not name its writer, but it closes by saying that ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’ (21:20) ‘wrote these things’ (21:24, KJV). Irenaeus said John, the Lord’s disciple who leaned on his breast, published it at Ephesus, and tradition identifies him as John the son of Zebedee; most modern scholars find that the evidence does not support this, and some, such as Martin Hengel and Richard Bauckham, credit it to John the elder, whom Papias mentions. Many also see later editing, with chapter 21 added after the Gospel was finished.
audience: Broad: Jews and Greeks, believers and seekers
setting: Ephesus, late first century; synagogue tension and early heresies
purpose: That you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:31)

author: Author uncertain; the writer of Luke (1:1); traditionally Luke, Paul’s companion
authorNote: Acts does not name its writer, but it begins by recalling ‘The former treatise’ written for Theophilus (1:1, KJV), so it comes from the writer of Luke, and some passages are told as ‘we’ (from 16:10). The Muratorian fragment and later tradition name Luke. Critical scholars have been roughly evenly divided on whether Paul’s companion Luke wrote it, reading the ‘we’ passages either as an eyewitness’s or as a source or literary device.
setting: Jerusalem to Rome across the empire, AD 30–62
purpose: To narrate the Spirit-empowered spread of the gospel from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth

author: Paul (named in 1:1)
authorNote: Paul names himself in 1:1, and Tertius, who wrote the letter down for him, adds his own greeting in 16:22. It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own, and early Christian writers treated it as undisputed.
date: c. AD 60, from Corinth (Ussher); others c. AD 57
audience: House churches in Rome, Jewish and Gentile
setting: Paul preparing to visit Rome en route to Spain; tension between Jewish and Gentile believers
purpose: To set out the gospel of righteousness by faith for Jew and Gentile alike

author: Paul (named in 1:1, with Sosthenes)
authorNote: Paul names himself with Sosthenes in 1:1 and writes the closing greeting in his own hand (16:21). It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own; Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth near the end of the 1st century, already directs the church to Paul’s letter.
date: c. AD 59, from Ephesus (Ussher); others c. AD 53–55
setting: Wealthy, immoral port city; a divided, gifted, immature church
purpose: To correct divisions and disorders and call the church to the way of the cross and love

author: Paul (named in 1:1, with Timothy)
authorNote: Paul names himself with Timothy in 1:1. It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own, and early Christian writers treated Paul’s letters as undisputed.
date: c. AD 60, from Macedonia (Ussher); others c. AD 55–56
setting: After a painful visit and letter; opponents challenging Paul's authority
purpose: To defend Paul's apostolic ministry and encourage reconciliation and generosity

author: Paul (named in 1:1)
authorNote: Paul names himself in 1:1 and notes that he writes with his own hand (6:11). It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own.
date: c. AD 58 (Ussher); others c. AD 48–55
setting: Judaizers insisting Gentiles be circumcised
purpose: To defend justification by faith apart from works of the law

author: Paul (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Paul names himself in 1:1 and writes as a prisoner (3:1), and the early church received the letter as his. Most critical scholars judge that a follower wrote it in Paul’s name after his death, on grounds of style and theology, while many evangelical scholars hold that Paul wrote it.
date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62; if by a later follower, c. AD 80–100
setting: Diverse Jew–Gentile congregations in a city of magic and pagan worship
purpose: To unfold God's eternal plan in Christ and the unity and holiness of the church

author: Paul (named in 1:1, with Timothy)
authorNote: Paul names himself with Timothy in 1:1 and writes from imprisonment (1:13). It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own, and Polycarp of Smyrna, writing to the same church, recalls that Paul wrote to them.
date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62
audience: Church in Philippi, a Roman colony
setting: Paul imprisoned; the church facing opposition and internal friction
purpose: To thank the church and call them to joyful, humble unity in Christ

author: Paul (named in 1:1, with Timothy); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Paul names himself with Timothy in 1:1 and writes the closing greeting in his own hand (4:18), and the early church received the letter as his. Scholars are sharply divided: many judge that a follower wrote it after Paul’s death, on grounds of vocabulary, style and theology, while others hold that Paul wrote it, and some, such as James Dunn, suggest that Timothy wrote it on Paul’s behalf while Paul was still alive.
date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62; if by a later follower, c. AD 70–80
setting: A church tempted by a syncretistic philosophy of asceticism and ritual
purpose: To show the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ
themes: Christ the image of the invisible God

author: Paul (named in 1:1, with Silvanus and Timothy)
authorNote: Paul names himself with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy in 1:1. It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own.
date: c. AD 54, from Corinth (Ussher); others c. AD 50–51; one of the earliest NT books
setting: Church planted quickly, then persecuted
purpose: To encourage a young church and clarify the return of Christ

author: Paul (named in 1:1, with Silvanus and Timothy); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Paul names himself with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy in 1:1 and stresses his own signature (3:17), and the early church received the letter as his. Scholars are roughly evenly divided: some see a later follower adapting 1 Thessalonians to a new situation, partly because its teaching on Christ’s coming differs from the first letter’s, while others hold that Paul wrote it.
date: c. AD 54, from Corinth (Ussher); others c. AD 51; if by a later follower, late 1st century
setting: Confusion that the Day of the Lord had already come
purpose: To correct end-time misunderstanding and confront idleness

author: Paul (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Paul is named in 1:1, and from Irenaeus (c. 180) onwards the church received the three Pastoral letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) as his, though Marcion’s collection (c. 140) left them out. Doubts were raised in the early 19th century, and most critical scholars now judge them the work of a later follower writing in Paul’s name, on grounds of vocabulary, style and church order; others, such as Carson and Moo, defend Paul’s authorship, some allowing for a secretary.
date: c. AD 65 (Ussher); others c. AD 62–64; if by a later follower, late 1st to mid 2nd century
audience: Timothy, leading the church at Ephesus
setting: False teaching, leadership disorder in Ephesus
purpose: To instruct on sound doctrine, church order and godly leadership

author: Paul (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Paul is named in 1:1, and from Irenaeus (c. 180) onwards the church received the three Pastoral letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) as his, though Marcion’s collection (c. 140) left them out. Doubts were raised in the early 19th century, and most critical scholars now judge them the work of a later follower writing in Paul’s name, on grounds of vocabulary, style and church order; others, such as Carson and Moo, defend Paul’s authorship, some allowing for a secretary.
date: c. AD 64–67, from prison in Rome; if by a later follower, late 1st to mid 2nd century
setting: Paul's final letter; desertion by many; Nero's persecution
purpose: To urge Timothy to guard the gospel and endure hardship

author: Paul (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: Paul is named in 1:1, and from Irenaeus (c. 180) onwards the church received the three Pastoral letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) as his, though Marcion’s collection (c. 140) left them out. Doubts were raised in the early 19th century, and most critical scholars now judge them the work of a later follower writing in Paul’s name, on grounds of vocabulary, style and church order; others, such as Carson and Moo, defend Paul’s authorship, some allowing for a secretary.
date: c. AD 65 (Ussher); others c. AD 62–64; if by a later follower, late 1st to mid 2nd century
setting: Crete's reputation for dishonesty; new churches needing elders
purpose: To set the churches in order and show how grace produces good works

author: Paul (named in verse 1, with Timothy)
authorNote: Paul names himself with Timothy in verse 1 and writes his promise to repay in his own hand (verse 19). It is one of the seven letters that scholars almost universally accept as Paul’s own, and Marcion’s collection of Paul’s letters (c. 140) already included it.
date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62
setting: Onesimus, Philemon's runaway slave, converted under Paul
purpose: To appeal for Onesimus to be received as a brother

author: Author uncertain; traditionally Paul; also proposed: Barnabas, Apollos, Luke, Priscilla
authorNote: The letter names no writer; the KJV title calls it Paul’s, but the oldest manuscripts head it simply ‘To Hebrews’. The Eastern church, from Clement of Alexandria and Origen, received it as Paul’s, though Origen judged that only God knows who wrote it; Tertullian named Barnabas, others Luke or Clement of Rome, and later Luther proposed Apollos and Harnack Priscilla. Most modern scholars doubt Paul wrote it, citing its polished Greek and the writer’s dependence on those who heard the Lord (2:3), and no alternative has won agreement.
date: Before c. AD 96 (1 Clement probably cites it); many date it before AD 70
audience: Jewish Christians tempted to drift back to Judaism
setting: Pressure and persecution; temple still functioning
purpose: To show Christ's superiority over Moses, priests and sacrifices, and to call for perseverance
outline: The Son supreme, greater than Moses

author: James (named in 1:1), traditionally the Lord’s brother; authorship widely disputed
authorNote: The writer calls himself ‘James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ’ (1:1, KJV); tradition identifies him as James the Lord’s brother, leader of the church in Jerusalem, who died in AD 62. Eusebius records that the letter was disputed in the early church, since not many of the ancients mention it. Modern scholars are divided: some defend James as the writer (perhaps with a secretary), some see his teaching edited later, and others a later writer using his name.
date: c. AD 40–62 if by James; many scholars c. AD 90–100
setting: Diaspora believers facing trials, poverty and partiality
purpose: To call for practical, wholehearted faith that works

author: Peter (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: The letter names ‘Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ’ (1:1, KJV) and says it was written ‘By Silvanus’ (5:12), from ‘Babylon’ (5:13), traditionally read as Rome. Its authorship was never challenged in antiquity, and from Irenaeus on the church accepted it as Peter’s. Many modern scholars think it was written in Peter’s name after his death, citing its polished Greek, while others hold that Peter wrote it, perhaps with Silvanus shaping the wording.
date: c. AD 64–67 if by Peter; many scholars c. AD 70–90
setting: Social hostility and scattered exiles under Roman rule
purpose: To encourage suffering believers to live as holy exiles with hope

author: Peter (named in 1:1); authorship widely disputed
authorNote: The letter names ‘Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ’ (1:1, KJV) and recalls the voice heard at the transfiguration (1:16–18). It was slow to be accepted: Origen, its first certain witness, called a second letter of Peter doubtful, and Eusebius listed it among the disputed books. Most modern scholars see it as written in Peter’s name, probably in the early second century, though some still defend Peter’s authorship.
date: c. AD 64–67 if by Peter; many scholars c. AD 100–150
setting: False teachers mocking the promise of Christ's return
purpose: To warn against false teachers and affirm the certainty of Christ's coming

author: Author uncertain; traditionally John the apostle; from the same circle as John’s Gospel
authorNote: The letter does not name its writer; it opens with eyewitness language about ‘the Word of life’ (1:1, KJV). Tradition credited it to John the apostle, and Eusebius counted it, with the Gospel, among the undisputed books. Many modern scholars, without naming a writer, see it as coming from the same Johannine circle as the Gospel.
setting: Secessionists denying Jesus came in the flesh
purpose: To give assurance of eternal life through tests of belief, obedience and love

author: Author uncertain; ‘the elder’ (1:1); traditionally John the apostle; some say John the elder
authorNote: The writer calls himself only ‘The elder’ (1:1, KJV). Tradition credits the letter to John the apostle, but Eusebius listed it among the disputed books, unsure whether it was by the evangelist or another of the same name, and Papias mentions a John the elder besides the apostle. Many modern scholars think it comes from a disciple in the apostle’s circle, and the elder’s identity remains uncertain.
audience: 'The elect lady and her children' (a church)
setting: Travelling teachers spreading false doctrine
purpose: To urge love in truth and refuse hospitality to deceivers

author: Author uncertain; ‘the elder’ (1:1); traditionally John the apostle; some say John the elder
authorNote: The writer calls himself only ‘The elder’, writing to Gaius (1:1, KJV). Tradition credits the letter to John the apostle, but Eusebius listed it among the disputed books, unsure whether it was by the evangelist or another of the same name, and Papias mentions a John the elder besides the apostle. Many modern scholars think it comes from a disciple in the apostle’s circle, and the elder’s identity remains uncertain.
setting: Diotrephes rejecting travelling missionaries
purpose: To commend Gaius' hospitality and rebuke Diotrephes

author: Jude (named in 1:1), traditionally the Lord’s brother; authorship widely disputed
authorNote: The writer calls himself ‘Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James’ (1:1, KJV), and he is generally identified as the Juda named among Jesus’ brothers (Mark 6:3), not one of the Twelve. Eusebius records that the letter was disputed in the early church. Many modern scholars see it as written in his name at the end of the first century or later, while others find their arguments not compelling and think Jude himself could have written it.
date: c. AD 65–80 if by Jude; many scholars c. AD 90 or later
setting: Libertine false teachers infiltrating the church
purpose: To contend for the faith once delivered to the saints

author: John (named in 1:1); traditionally the apostle; authorship widely disputed
authorNote: The writer names himself John, on ‘the isle that is called Patmos’ (1:9, KJV), but never claims to be an apostle. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus identified him as John the apostle; Dionysius of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius, argued from its Greek and style that it was another John, and Eusebius suggested John the elder, known to Papias. Many modern scholars doubt that he also wrote the Fourth Gospel.
date: c. AD 95–96 (late in Domitian’s reign); some date it before AD 70
setting: Roman imperial cult; persecution under Domitian (or Nero)
purpose: To unveil Jesus Christ as the risen Lord of history and encourage faithful endurance until the new creation
